claims.claim: You must take out basic mandatory health insurance within three months of taking up residence in Switzerland.
If you take out insurance within this three-month window, your coverage takes effect retroactively from the date you took up residence.
Consequently, you are covered for medical treatment received since your arrival, and you must pay premiums retroactively back to that date.
If you register after the three-month deadline without an excuse, your insurance coverage only begins on the date you actually enroll.
Any healthcare costs incurred between your arrival and your enrollment date will not be reimbursed.
You will be charged a penalty surcharge (*Prämienzuschlag*) on your premiums for unexcused delays.
This surcharge ranges from 30% to 50% of your premium and is charged for double the duration of the delay, up to a maximum of five years.
The surcharge may be reduced if it causes personal hardship.
The cantons are responsible for enforcing the insurance requirement.
If you fail to enroll on time, the designated cantonal authority will automatically assign you to a health insurer.

Cantonal authorities (such as the cantonal health department or municipal social insurance office) oversee compliance with mandatory insurance and have the authority to assign you to a health insurer if you fail to choose one.

claims.claim: Pour avoir droit aux indemnités de chômage en Suisse, vous devez en principe avoir exercé une activité salariée soumise à cotisation pendant au moins 12 mois.

Certaines périodes d'inactivité sont assimilées à des périodes de cotisation, notamment en cas de service militaire ou de protection civile suisse, de maladie ou d'accident sans salaire sous contrat de travail, ou de maternité.

Des dérogations existent : vous pouvez être libéré des conditions relatives à la période de cotisation si vous n'avez pas pu travailler pendant plus de 12 mois au total au cours des deux dernières années en raison d'une formation, d'une maladie, d'un accident ou d'une maternité.

claims.claim: During the probation period, there is no statutory protection against dismissal due to illness.
The employment relationship can be terminated at any time during the probation period with a notice period of seven days.

After the probation period, the employee is protected by a statutory waiting period (Sperrfrist) against dismissal if they are unable to work fully or partially due to illness without fault of their own.
The duration of the protection period is 30 days in the first year of service, 90 days from the second to the fifth year of service, and 180 days from the sixth year of service.
A dismissal issued by the employer during an ongoing protection period is null and void (nichtig) and therefore legally ineffective.

If the employee was already dismissed before the illness, the dismissal is valid, but the notice period is suspended for the duration of the incapacity to work (up to the end of the protection period) and resumes afterward.

If the employment relationship normally ends on a fixed date (e.g., end of the month), and that date does not coincide with the end of the resumed notice period, the period is extended to the next such fixed termination date.
